Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Vignette:
Robert, a 55-year-old fashion designer, had carried the weight of his childhood for decades. He remembered the house, not as a sanctuary, but as a place of unpredictable tension. What he could recall were fragmented flashes: the sudden, unnerving quiet that would descend upon the home, a stillness that always preceded his caregiver’s violent outbursts. He learned to brace himself, his small body tensing, waiting for the inevitable. Sometimes, the memory would come back to him with a strange, almost detached quality, as if he were watching a scene unfold for a stranger, feeling completely numb. Other times, a wave of intense guilt would wash over him, a persistent, gnawing feeling that he had somehow failed, that he should have done something, anything, to stop it. He had tried many times to piece together a clear, coherent story of what happened, even just for himself, but the details remained stubbornly elusive, a jumble of fear and confusion.

Over the years, the echoes of those early experiences manifested in his daily life. The sudden, unexpected touch from a colleague in his bustling fashion studio, perhaps a hand on his shoulder as they discussed a design, would send a jolt of alarm through him, making him flinch violently. He’d learned to anticipate such moments, keeping a watchful distance, but the reaction was involuntary and immediate. Even in the quiet solitude of his apartment, a space he had meticulously designed for comfort, he felt perpetually on guard. The absence of sound, particularly at night, was not peaceful but menacing; an unusual silence made him feel a dangerous event was imminent, his senses heightened, listening for any disruption.

His internal world was equally turbulent. Robert had long since come to believe that his childhood had permanently changed him for the worse, leaving an indelible mark on his very being. This conviction fed into a deep-seated mistrust; he was certain that people couldn't truly be trusted, and that anyone could turn on him without warning. This belief had slowly eroded his marriage, contributing to his eventual divorce, as his wife grew weary of his emotional distance and guardedness. He found himself dwelling endlessly on what his caregiver had done to him, replaying the injustices in his mind, but also obsessively scrutinizing his own past actions, dwelling on what he had done wrong, searching for a fault that might explain his suffering. The intensity of his reactions—the sudden fright, the constant vigilance—sometimes made him fear he was going crazy, a terrifying thought that only deepened his sense of isolation.

Sleep offered little respite. Robert had developed a complex ritual around bedtime, actively avoiding situations or times of day that tended to bring on nightmares. He would stay up late in his studio, meticulously reviewing designs or sketching new ideas, preferring exhaustion to the vivid, terrifying replays that often accompanied sleep. This habit, formed over decades, meant he often started his workdays already drained, impacting his focus and creativity. The constant internal battles, the pervasive sense of threat, and the relentless rumination had taken a toll. He had finally sought help, driven by a growing weariness and the quiet desperation that perhaps, after all these years, there might be a way to live without the constant fear that lurked just beneath the surface of his carefully curated life. What frightened him most was the idea that this was simply who he was, and that he might never truly escape the shadow of his past.
